explain.say: When you heat a pan of water on a hob, only the bottom touches the heat. Yet soon all the water is warm, carried round by a convection current.

faq.a: It is a loop of moving liquid or gas that carries heat. Warm fluid rises, cools and sinks, then gets warmed and rises again.
Warm water expands, so it is less dense than the cooler water around it. The cooler, denser water sinks beneath it and pushes it up, like a cork floating.
No. In a solid the particles stay in place and only vibrate, so they cannot flow round in a current. Solids pass heat by conduction instead.

faq.q: How can I see convection in a pan?
faq.a: Drop a few grains of rice, or a pinch of crushed herbs, into water as it heats. You will see them carried up in the middle and down at the sides.

faq.q: Where else do convection currents happen?
faq.a: In warm air rising from a radiator, in sea breezes, in the oceans, deep inside the Earth's mantle and in the outer layers of the Sun.

facts: Convection only happens in fluids, meaning liquids and gases, because their particles can move from place to place.
A radiator warms a room mainly by convection, despite its name.
